We provide interior design consultation, concept development, material specification, project management, and related creative services. The specific scope, deliverables, timeline, and fees for each project are defined in a separate proposal or engagement letter provided before work begins.
All proposals are valid for 30 days from the date of issue unless otherwise stated. We reserve the right to adjust fees if the scope of work changes materially after a proposal has been accepted.

p: How we collect, use, and protect your personal information when you visit our website or engage our design services.

We collect information you provide directly when you fill out our contact form, subscribe to our newsletter, or correspond with us via email. This includes your name, email address, phone number, project details, and any other information you choose to share.

We also automatically collect certain technical data when you visit our website, including your IP address, browser type, device information, pages visited, and time spent on the site. This data is collected through cookies and similar technologies.

We use the information we collect to respond to your inquiries, provide design consultations, send project proposals, and communicate about ongoing work. If you have subscribed, we may also send occasional newsletters with design insights and studio updates.

Technical data is used to analyze website performance, improve user experience, and understand how visitors interact with our content. We do not use this data for advertising or sell it to third parties.
We do not sell, rent, or trade your personal information. We may share data with trusted service providers who assist in operating our website, managing email communications, or processing analytics.
These providers include our web hosting platform (Framer), email service (ConvertKit), and analytics tool (Plausible). Each is bound by their own privacy policies and data protection obligations.

Our website uses essential cookies to ensure basic functionality. We use Plausible Analytics, which is privacy-focused and does not use cookies for tracking. You can disable cookies through your browser settings at any time.

We retain your personal information only for as long as necessary to fulfill the purposes outlined in this policy. Contact form submissions and project inquiries are retained for up to 24 months. Newsletter subscriber data is retained until you unsubscribe.

You have the right to access, correct, or delete your personal data at any time. You may also request a copy of the data we hold about you or ask us to restrict its processing. To exercise any of these rights, contact us at hello@aveondesign.com.

If you are located in the European Union or United Kingdom, you have additional rights under the GDPR, including the right to data portability and the right to lodge a complaint with your local data protection authority.
If you are a California resident, the CCPA provides you with additional rights regarding your personal information, including the right to know what data we collect and the right to request deletion.

We implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect your personal information against unauthorized access, alteration, disclosure, or destruction. Our website uses SSL encryption to secure data transmitted between your browser and our servers.

Our website and services are not directed at individuals under the age of 16. We do not knowingly collect personal information from children. If we become aware that we have collected data from a child, we will delete it promptly.

We may update this privacy policy from time to time. Any changes will be posted on this page with an updated revision date. Continued use of our website after changes are posted constitutes acceptance of the updated policy.

/guia/preguntas-frecuentes.description: Our Elm Grove Residence wins the 2026 INDA Award for Residential Interior Design.

p: Our Elm Grove Residence project has been recognized with the 2026 INDA Award for Residential Interior Design. A proud moment for the studio.

We are honored to share that our Elm Grove Residence has been awarded the 2026 INDA Award for Residential Interior Design. For a studio that started six years ago in a converted warehouse with two desks and a coffee machine, this recognition means everything.

The award was announced at the INDA ceremony in Milan on January 18th, alongside projects from studios we have admired for years. Standing on that stage and hearing our project described as a benchmark for thoughtful residential renovation was surreal.

Elm Grove is a 2,800 sq ft renovation of a 1920s bungalow in the inner suburbs of Melbourne. The clients, Claire and Tom Ashford, came to us with a deceptively simple brief: make it feel like it has always been here.

The original home had beautiful bones — high ceilings in the front rooms, original timber floors, and a graceful roofline — but decades of patchwork renovations had buried them under plasterboard, carpet, and fluorescent lighting. Our job was not to impose a new identity but to uncover the one that was already there.

We retained the original facade and roofline while completely rethinking the interior layout. The rear of the house was opened into a single kitchen-dining-living zone that flows directly into the garden. Key material choices — recycled brick salvaged from a demolished factory, brushed limestone sourced from a quarry in regional Victoria, and white oak joinery milled by a local craftsman — connect the old and new seamlessly.

Every material was selected not just for how it looked, but for how it would age. The brick will darken with time. The limestone will develop a soft patina. The oak will mellow from honey to amber. In ten years, these rooms will look better than they do today.

The jury praised the project for its restraint and sensitivity to context. Their citation noted that the design demonstrates how renovation can be an act of preservation rather than erasure, and that the material palette shows a maturity and coherence that elevates the everyday experience of living.

The judges specifically mentioned the kitchen island — a 4.5-meter slab of honed Elba marble that anchors the open-plan space. They called it the heart of the home, noting that its scale and materiality give the room a center of gravity that makes the entire floor plan feel grounded.

This award belongs to the entire team. To our designers who spent months refining every detail. To our builders who executed the vision with precision and care. To our stone mason who has been with us since our second project. And most importantly, to Claire and Tom, who trusted us to reimagine their home and gave us the creative freedom to do it properly.

We are not slowing down. This recognition reinforces our belief that residential design matters — that the spaces where people raise their families, share meals, and find rest deserve the same attention and craft as any public building or commercial project.
We are grateful for the recognition and excited about what lies ahead.

/guia/dia-de-campo.description: Design strategies for compact apartments and small homes that prioritize function without sacrificing beauty.
h1: Small Spaces, Big Ideas: Designing Under 800 Square Feet
h2: Furniture That Works as Hard as You Do
h4: Stay inspired with design insights!
Start A New Project to Grow your business!

The Case for Limewash — And Why We Keep Specifying It
From Brief to Build: How We Approach Every New Project
p: Compact living doesn't mean compromising on design. The best small spaces feel considered, not cramped — here's how we approach them.
Some of our most rewarding projects have been the smallest. When every square foot matters, there is no room for indecision or filler. Every element earns its place or it goes.

Small space design is not about tricks, hacks, or clever storage solutions borrowed from Instagram. It is about rigor. Understanding exactly what a household needs and delivering that with precision, clarity, and zero compromise on quality.

We recently completed a 650 sq ft apartment for a couple who both work from home. The brief was impossible on paper: two workspaces, a full kitchen, a dining area for four, generous storage, and a bedroom that did not feel like an afterthought. We delivered all of it. The key was eliminating everything that did not serve a daily function and designing the things that remained to work twice as hard.

The most common mistake in small spaces is thinking only in plan. Walls are real estate. Ceilings are real estate. The space above doorframes, below windows, and behind headboards — all of it is usable if you design for it.

Floor-to-ceiling built-ins are the single most impactful investment in a compact home. A single wall of custom oak cabinetry can replace a wardrobe, bookshelf, desk, and media unit. One surface, four functions, zero floor space consumed.

We design joinery with concealed handles, push-to-open mechanisms, and integrated lighting so the wall reads as architecture rather than furniture. The result is a room that feels larger because the storage has disappeared into the envelope.

In studio apartments, raising the bed onto a platform creates usable volume underneath. We have built platforms with pull-out drawers, concealed shoe storage, and even a retractable desk. The sleeping area gains a sense of enclosure and privacy, while the floor below gains square footage.

In larger homes, you can shift materials between rooms and nobody notices. In compact spaces, every material transition is felt. Consistency is not just aesthetic preference — it is a spatial strategy.

We limit compact spaces to three dominant tones: a primary surface tone (usually floor and large joinery), a secondary accent (hardware, lighting, textiles), and a recessive background (walls and ceiling). This creates visual calm. The moment you introduce too many competing materials, a small space feels cluttered regardless of how little furniture is in it.
In compact homes, furniture selection is closer to spatial planning than decoration. Every piece needs to justify its footprint.

A dining table that doubles as a workspace. A sofa with integrated storage. A bed frame with built-in drawers. A bench that conceals shoes, bags, and umbrellas. These are not compromises. They are smarter solutions designed for how people actually live in small spaces.
The homes we design under these principles tend to feel larger than their measurements suggest. Clients tell us their apartments feel spacious. That is not magic. It is editing.

/guia/como-llegar.description: How orientation, glazing, and layout decisions shape the way we experience residential spaces. A deep dive into designing with light.
h1: Why Natural Light Changes Everything in Interior Design
h3: The Window as a Design Element
h4: Stay inspired with design insights!
Start A New Project to Grow your business!
Get quarterly notes on new work, materials, and behind-the-scenes process
h5: The Case for Limewash — And Why We Keep Specifying It
From Brief to Build: How We Approach Every New Project
Small Spaces, Big Ideas: Designing Under 800 Square Feet
p: Light doesn't just illuminate a room — it defines it. How orientation, glazing, and layout decisions shape the way we experience space.

Natural light is the one material in interior design that costs nothing, weighs nothing, and transforms everything. It shifts the mood of a room by the hour. It changes how colors read on walls, how textures feel underfoot, and whether a space invites you in or pushes you away.

When we begin a new project, the first thing we study isn't the floor plan. It's the sun path. Where does morning light enter? Which walls catch golden hour? Where do shadows collect in winter? These questions shape every decision that follows.

A north-facing living room in London behaves completely differently from a south-facing one in Melbourne. The quality of light — its color temperature, intensity, and duration — dictates material choices, paint tones, and furniture placement.

We categorize rooms by the light they receive. A morning room gets cool, blue-toned light that pairs well with warm timber and soft textiles. An afternoon room gets saturated, golden light that can overwhelm warm finishes and works better with cooler stones and muted plaster.
Understanding this distinction prevents the most common mistake in residential design: selecting materials under showroom lighting and being surprised when they look different at home.
Windows are not just openings. They are frames. We treat every window as a compositional decision — what does it reveal, what does it hide, and how does the light it admits change across the seasons?

Not every project comes with floor-to-ceiling glazing. In older buildings, windows are often small, deep-set, and irregularly placed. The goal is not to fight the architecture. It is to amplify what exists.
Light-toned lime plaster walls bounce light deeper into a room. Polished concrete floors reflect it upward. Strategically placed mirrors double the perceived window area without structural work.

Internal rooms do not have to be dark. Glazed partitions, transom windows above doors, and open shelving between rooms allow light to travel through a floor plan. We recently used fluted glass panels to bring daylight from a kitchen into a windowless hallway.

Studies consistently show that access to natural light improves mood, sleep quality, and productivity. In residential design, this is the difference between a home that feels alive and one that feels like a sealed box.

Clients who move from dark apartments into light-filled spaces report sleeping better within the first week. Children do homework more willingly at a sunlit desk. Kitchens with morning light make breakfast feel less rushed.

Before we select a single finish, we understand the light. We visit the site at three different times of day. We photograph every room at morning, midday, and dusk. Only then do we begin designing. Light is the starting point, not an afterthought.

h1: From Brief to Build: How We Approach Every New Project
h4: Stay inspired with design insights!

p: A look inside our design process — from the first client conversation to the final walkthrough. No two projects are the same, but the framework is.

The first meeting is never about mood boards or Pinterest links. It is about understanding how someone actually lives. What time do they wake up? Where do they drop their keys? Do they cook every night or order in three times a week? Do they work from home? Do guests stay often?

These details matter more than any aesthetic preference. A beautiful kitchen that does not suit your cooking habits is a failed kitchen. A stunning home office that faces a noisy street is a room you will never use.

We visit the space at least twice before presenting anything. The first visit is about observation — how light moves through the rooms, where the noise comes from, what the views offer. The second is about measurement and documentation. We photograph everything, scan the floor plan, and note every service point, structural element, and quirk.

Clients often know what they want but struggle to articulate it. Someone who says they want a minimalist home might actually mean they want less clutter, not less furniture. Someone who says they love color might mean they want one bold wall, not a rainbow. Our job is to read between the lines and translate feelings into spatial decisions.

Once we understand the daily rhythms of a household, we develop a spatial concept. This is not decoration. It is architecture at a human scale. We map circulation patterns, identify where natural light falls, and define zones for activity, rest, and transition.

The concept is presented as a series of spatial diagrams, material palettes, and reference images. We do not show specific furniture at this stage. The idea needs to be right before we get into specifics. Clients receive a physical concept book with fabric swatches, stone samples, and timber offcuts alongside the drawings.

Materials are selected in person whenever possible. We visit stone yards, timber suppliers, and fabric showrooms with clients. Photographs lie. You need to see how travertine catches afternoon light, or how a wool boucle feels against skin. We build physical sample boards for every project.

We work with a small network of trusted builders, joiners, and artisans. Relationships matter here. We have been working with the same stone mason for seven years and the same joiner for five. That continuity shows in the quality of the finish.

Site visits happen weekly during construction. Details get resolved in real time, not over email chains. We maintain a rolling punch list that tracks every open item, and nothing gets signed off until it meets our standard. Clients receive a photo update after every visit.

The final walkthrough is our favorite part of any project. We style the space with soft furnishings, place the books on the shelves, light the candles, and step back. Seeing a client step into their finished home for the first time — that moment of recognition, of feeling like the space already belongs to them — is why we do this work.

/guia/fin-de-semana.title: The Case for Limewash — And Why We Keep Specifying It
/guia/fin-de-semana.description: Why limewash walls are making a comeback in modern interior design and how this ancient technique adds depth no flat paint can match.
h1: The Case for Limewash — And Why We Keep Specifying It
h2: A Material That Predates Modern Design
Application: Where Most Projects Go Wrong
h3: How It Reads in a Room
h4: Stay inspired with design insights!

h5: Why Natural Light Changes Everything in Interior Design
From Brief to Build: How We Approach Every New Project
Small Spaces, Big Ideas: Designing Under 800 Square Feet
p: Limewash isn't a trend. It's a centuries-old finish that adds depth, texture, and warmth that flat paint simply can't replicate.

Every few years, limewash gets rediscovered by design media and declared the next big thing. But for studios that work with traditional materials, it never left. Limewash has been used on interior and exterior walls for centuries across the Mediterranean, North Africa, and Northern Europe.

It is mineral-based, breathable, and ages beautifully. Unlike acrylic paint, which sits on a surface like plastic film, limewash bonds chemically with the substrate and develops a living patina over time. The finish deepens. It softens. It becomes part of the wall rather than a layer on top of it.

The appeal is simple: depth. A limewashed wall catches light differently at every angle. It shifts between warm and cool tones depending on the time of day. It has movement and variation that flat paint can never achieve.

Limewash is made from slaked lime, water, and natural pigments. When applied, the calcium hydroxide reacts with carbon dioxide in the air to form calcium carbonate — essentially turning back into limestone on the wall. This carbonation process is what gives limewash its characteristic chalky, mineral texture.

The result is a surface that breathes. Moisture passes through rather than being trapped behind a paint film, which makes limewash naturally resistant to mold and mildew in properly ventilated spaces.

In a residential context, limewash translates to rooms that feel calm and textured without adding physical dimension. The walls do the work. A limewashed bedroom in a warm putty tone feels like being wrapped in something soft. A limewashed hallway in raw white has a quiet luminosity that no eggshell paint can replicate.

We use limewash most often in living rooms, bedrooms, and entry halls — spaces where warmth without distraction matters. It pairs beautifully with natural timber, linen upholstery, brushed brass hardware, and handmade ceramics.

In wet areas, we tend toward tadelakt or microcement instead. Both offer a similar mineral aesthetic but are engineered for moisture resistance. Tadelakt, a traditional Moroccan plaster, is waterproof when burnished with olive oil soap and works beautifully around sinks, showers, and splashbacks.

Limewash is not forgiving of poor preparation. The substrate needs to be porous — raw plaster, unsealed brick, or lime render. It will not adhere properly to sealed surfaces, vinyl paint, or gypsum board without extensive preparation.

Application is done by hand in cross-hatch strokes, which is what creates the characteristic clouded finish. We always recommend two to three coats for residential walls, building up opacity gradually rather than forcing full coverage in one pass.

The applicator matters as much as the product. We work with specialist plasterers who understand lime-based materials and can control the variation between strokes. A skilled hand produces walls that look effortless. An unskilled one produces walls that look patchy.

Limewash dries significantly lighter than it appears when wet. We always test three to four coats on a 1-meter sample area and live with it for at least 48 hours before committing to a full room. The color continues to develop over the first few weeks as the carbonation process completes.

/guia/estadia-vacacional.title: Warm Minimalism Is Not a Style — It's a Discipline
/guia/estadia-vacacional.description: How warm minimalism balances restraint with character through careful material choices, tonal layering, and intentional imperfection.
h1: Warm Minimalism Is Not a Style — It's a Discipline
h2: The Problem With the Word Minimalism
What Warm Actually Means in Design
h4: Stay inspired with design insights!
Start A New Project to Grow your business!
Get quarterly notes on new work, materials, and behind-the-scenes process
h5: Why Natural Light Changes Everything in Interior Design
The Case for Limewash — And Why We Keep Specifying It
From Brief to Build: How We Approach Every New Project
p: Minimalism with soul. Why stripping back doesn't mean stripping away character, and how we bring warmth to restrained spaces.
Minimalism has an image problem. People hear the word and picture cold white rooms with a single sad cactus on a concrete shelf. That is not minimalism. That is emptiness dressed up as intention.

True minimalism is about care. Every object, material, and surface is chosen deliberately. Nothing is there by default, by habit, or because it was on sale. The room has exactly what it needs and nothing more. But what it has is exceptional.

Somewhere between Scandinavian design magazines and social media, minimalism became about absence rather than presence. The goal shifted from intentional living to performative emptiness. People removed everything from their homes to photograph them, then put it all back when the camera turned off. That is not a design philosophy. That is staging.
Warmth in interior design comes from three things: natural materials, tonal depth, and imperfection. Remove any one of these and a minimal space tips into coldness.

Timber with visible grain. Stone with natural veining. Linen that wrinkles. Brass that develops a patina. Leather that softens with age. These materials carry life. They change over time. They respond to touch, light, and use. A hand-plastered wall is minimal but warm. A machine-smooth drywall painted white is minimal but cold. The difference is not complexity. It is character.

Warm minimalism rarely uses pure white. Instead, we work with a tonal range: raw plasters in putty and bone, timbers in honey and ash, stones in warm grey and sand. The palette reads as quiet rather than blank. Layering these tones creates depth without adding visual noise.

A perfectly smooth surface reads as manufactured. A slightly uneven plaster wall reads as human. Handmade tiles with subtle variation. A dining table with a visible wood knot. A ceramic vase with a thumbprint from the potter. These imperfections are not flaws. They are proof that someone made this with their hands.

Warm minimalism requires brutal editing. For every object that stays, three were considered and rejected. The bookshelf has thirty books, not three hundred. The kitchen counter holds a kettle and a cutting board, not every appliance you own.

This is not about deprivation. It is about making room for the things that actually matter to be seen, used, and appreciated. A single vase of wildflowers on an otherwise empty table has more impact than a crowded mantelpiece of decorative objects.

The spaces we design under this philosophy tend to age remarkably well. Materials develop character rather than deteriorating. The absence of trend-driven elements means the interior does not date within five years.

Clients report that their homes feel calmer. Easier to maintain. More enjoyable to return to at the end of a long day. They buy fewer things because everything they own has a place and a purpose. They entertain more because the space feels generous rather than cluttered.
That is the real promise of warm minimalism. Not aesthetic purity. Not Instagram perfection. Just daily peace in a space that works.

p: Architecture firm workplace in a converted warehouse. Exposed concrete, birch plywood, and a central materials library.

The existing space was a generic open-plan office with fluorescent lighting, grey carpet tiles, and zero personality. The firm needed a workspace that reflected the quality of their own architectural output.

Acoustically, the space was a disaster. The concrete ceiling and hard surfaces meant phone calls bled across the entire floor. Focused work was nearly impossible, and client meetings required booking external venues because the office felt unprofessional.

We exposed the original concrete ceiling and brick walls, then layered in warm interventions: birch plywood workstations, felt acoustic panels in earthy tones, and a central materials library built from blackened steel shelving. A client lounge with a fireplace anchors the entry.

Acoustic zones were created through ceiling baffles, floor-level planters, and a glazed meeting room with operable walls that can open into the main studio for all-hands gatherings. The lighting system alternates between task-focused and ambient modes depending on the time of day.

Staff satisfaction surveys showed a 40% improvement in workplace comfort. The studio has since been used as a venue for client presentations and industry events, generating additional revenue for the firm.

The materials library has become a talking point with visiting clients and a practical resource for the design team. Three firms in the same building have since approached the studio about redesigning their own offices, citing the Arch Studio space as direct inspiration.

p: Boutique hotel conversion of a Lisbon textile warehouse. 14 individually designed rooms with Portuguese marble and blackened steel.
The building had been vacant for three years. Water damage, outdated electrical, and a fragmented layout across four floors made it a complex renovation with a tight timeline.

The client also faced strict heritage regulations that prevented changes to the street-facing facade and original staircase. Every design decision had to work within these constraints while still delivering a contemporary hospitality experience that could compete with established Lisbon hotels.

We preserved the original iron columns and timber trusses while inserting contemporary interventions in tadelakt, blackened steel, and Portuguese marble. Each of the 14 rooms was designed individually with its own palette and character.

The ground floor was reimagined as a public-facing lobby bar with a double-height ceiling, terrazzo flooring, and a custom reception desk carved from a single block of Estremoz marble. Lighting was designed room by room with local ceramicist Ana Brito, who created bespoke fixtures for every guest room.

The hotel launched at 94% occupancy in its first month and was featured in Monocle and Wallpaper* within six weeks of opening. It has since become a reference project for hospitality clients approaching the studio.

Revenue per available room exceeded projections by 30% in the first quarter, driven largely by the lobby bar becoming a destination for locals. The project demonstrated that heritage constraints, when embraced rather than fought, produce spaces with a depth that new builds rarely achieve.

p: Chef-owned modern bistro in Tokyo. Shou sugi ban timber, hand-troweled plaster, and custom brass lighting.

The previous tenant had left the space stripped bare. Exposed ductwork, concrete slab floors, and zero acoustic treatment meant every sound bounced. The owners had a strong culinary vision but no clear idea of how the dining experience should feel spatially.

The floor plan was long and narrow with only one street-facing window, making natural light scarce. The kitchen extraction system needed a complete overhaul to meet Tokyo's strict ventilation codes, and the budget was tight for a space that needed to feel premium from day one.

We divided the space into three distinct zones — an open kitchen counter, a main dining room, and a private alcove for six — using material shifts instead of walls. Shou sugi ban timber panels absorb sound while adding warmth. A custom brass light installation runs the length of the bar, casting a warm amber glow across hand-troweled plaster walls.

The private alcove is separated by a floor-to-ceiling curtain in raw silk, creating intimacy without permanent division. We designed every piece of furniture in-house: low-backed dining chairs in blackened ash, a 3-meter bar counter in volcanic stone, and banquette seating upholstered in indigo linen. The kitchen pass was raised to create a theater of cooking visible from every seat.

The restaurant reached full reservation capacity within two weeks of opening and was named in TimeOut Tokyo's Best New Restaurants list. The private dining alcove now generates 20% of total revenue through exclusive tasting menu bookings.

The owners have since commissioned us for their second venue, a sake bar in Shibuya, citing the design as the single biggest factor in Noma's early success. Guests consistently mention the atmosphere in reviews — proof that hospitality design is never just about the food.

/espacios/galeria-asador.description: Clifftop holiday home on the NSW coast. Raw limestone, whitewashed timber, and floor-to-ceiling ocean views.
h2: A full interior renovation of a 1920s bungalow for a young family of four. The brief was to preserve the home's heritage character while opening the floor plan for modern family living.

p: Clifftop holiday home on the NSW coast. Raw limestone, whitewashed timber, and floor-to-ceiling ocean views.

The home sat on a stunning clifftop site but the interiors completely ignored the surroundings. Heavy drapes blocked the ocean views, dark timber paneling made every room feel enclosed, and the layout forced circulation away from the coast-facing rooms.

Salt air corrosion had damaged most of the existing fixtures and hardware. The timber window frames were warped, several rooms had persistent damp issues from poor ventilation, and the kitchen and bathrooms hadn't been updated since the 1990s. The home needed to be rebuilt for coastal conditions, not just redecorated.

We stripped the interior back to its shell and rebuilt around the view. Every living space now faces the ocean. We used raw limestone floors, whitewashed timber ceilings, and floor-to-ceiling glazing to blur the boundary between inside and out. Furniture was kept low and natural — linen, rattan, and brushed teak.

All materials were selected for salt-air durability: marine-grade stainless steel hardware, powder-coated aluminum window frames, and sealed limestone that resists moisture penetration. The master bedroom opens onto a private terrace with an outdoor shower, and a covered veranda runs the full width of the house for year-round coastal living.

The home is now used year-round instead of seasonally. The owners report hosting three times more guests than before, and the project was shortlisted for the 2025 Australian Interior Design Awards in the Residential category.

The veranda has become the most-used space in the house, serving as an outdoor dining room from October through April. The Whitmores say they no longer think of it as a holiday home — they're considering making it their permanent residence.

h2: A full interior renovation of a 1920s bungalow for a young family of four. The brief was to preserve the home's heritage character while opening the floor plan for modern family living.

p: Full interior renovation of a heritage bungalow in Melbourne. Recycled brick, limestone, and white oak joinery for a young family.
The original layout was dark and compartmentalized with low ceilings and minimal connection to the garden. Load-bearing walls limited options for opening up the rear of the house.

Beyond the structural constraints, decades of patchwork renovations had left the home with inconsistent floor levels, outdated plumbing, and electrical wiring that didn't meet current code. The family needed a space that could handle two young children while still feeling calm and considered.

We worked with a structural engineer to remove two internal walls and introduce a steel beam, creating an open kitchen-dining-living zone. Recycled brick, brushed limestone floors, and white oak joinery tie the original front rooms to the new rear extension.

The kitchen was designed as the heart of the home with a 4.5-meter island in honed Elba marble, integrated storage to keep clutter out of sight, underfloor heating throughout, and a concealed mudroom at the side entry for school bags and wet weather gear.

A home that feels both new and familiar. The family spends most of their time in the open-plan living area, exactly as intended. The indoor-outdoor flow transformed how they use the garden, turning it into an extension of the kitchen.

p: We started with a belief that great design begins with how people actually live. Six years later, that conviction drives every project we take on — residential, commercial, and everything in between.
In 2020, Grant Mitchell and Cole Bradford left their positions at a top-tier architecture firm with one idea: design should start with people, not Pinterest boards.

They set up in a converted warehouse in Brooklyn with nothing but two drafting tables and a shared belief that residential design deserved the same rigor as commercial work. The first project was a 400 sq ft apartment. The approach hasn't changed since.
Every project starts the same way — a long conversation. We ask about your mornings, your routines, how you use light, where you feel most at home. The answers shape everything.

We don't believe in signature styles. Your space should feel like you, not like us. Our role is to translate how you live into materials, proportions, and details that make daily life feel effortless.

We only specify materials we've touched, tested, and trust. No trend-chasing, no disposable finishes. Every surface in our projects is chosen to age with grace — limestone that patinas, brass that deepens, timber that mellows.
The result is spaces that look better at year five than they did at week one. That's not an accident. It's a commitment we make on every single project.
